Apologies for the confusion! Let me set the scene properly from the start.

The world is one of deep stone and cold iron, where the old gods are honoured in mountain temples and the mineshafts run dark and long beneath the peaks. Greyhollow is a mining town carved into a frost-bitten mountainside, and its people know the mountain's moods better than most. Brakka Ironvein, a hill dwarf fighter, has spent the last six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father there, keeping watch over the faithful and the forge-fires alike.

Three days ago, three miners descended into the North Works, the old galleries sealed off a generation ago. None returned. Last night a fourth man stumbled out of the dark alone, raving about lights that walk, and died before dawn. The town council has decided to brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. But Prior Hessa, the old dwarf who leads the temple, asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back.

It is late afternoon on the tenth of Frost. Brakka stands at the mine mouth, a hooded lantern borrowed from the temple in one hand. The opening is a rough-cut arch in the mountainside, old timber framing blackened with age. A cold draft breathes out from the darkness beyond, carrying the faint smell of wet stone and something else, something stale and old. The tracks of the mine cart rails vanish into the black. Behind Brakka, the grey light of a fading autumn day.

What does Brakka do?

I check the ground at the mine mouth for fresh tracks and any sign of where the three miners went in, then light the hooded lantern and keep my shield up as I step onto the cart rails. Prior Hessa's trust is riding on this, so I'll move slowly and watch for that stale smell getting stronger.
dice Brakka's Survival check to find tracks at the mine mouth: 1d20+2 = 1d20 [7] + 2 = 9

You kneel at the mine mouth, lantern set down for a moment, and study the ground. The stone dust and gravel show signs of passage, but the tracks are muddled. You can make out the parallel grooves of the mine cart rails, and there are boot prints, but they overlap and smear where several people have walked back and forth. You can tell that multiple people entered recently, heading in, but the exact number and whether any came back out is hard to say from here.

You light the hooded lantern. Its warm glow pushes back the shadows, the shuttered beam casting a cone of amber light ahead. Shield raised, you step onto the cart rails and begin to walk into the mountain.

The air cools immediately. The smell is stronger now, that stale, old scent like a sealed room left for decades. Your boots crunch on the gravel between the rails. The timber supports pass overhead in a rhythm, some newer and some so old the wood has turned grey and soft. The walls are rough-cut stone, glistening with moisture in the lantern light. The tunnel slopes gently downward, curving slightly to the left.

After about fifty feet, the tunnel opens into a small chamber where two passages branch off. To the left, the tunnel continues, and you can see old timber doors hanging open, marked with a faded sign. To the right, a narrower passage descends more steeply, and from it comes a faint, cold draft carrying that stale smell more strongly.

The lantern light flickers in the draft. What do you do?

I'll step over to the left passage first and look at the faded sign on the timber doors, holding the lantern up to read it. Then I'll check the floor near the branch for any fresh boot prints or cart marks leading toward the steeper right passage, since that's where the stale smell is strongest.

You step to the left passage and hold the lantern up to the timber doors. The wood is old and warped, hanging crooked on rusted hinges. Above them, a wooden sign is nailed to the frame. The paint has mostly peeled away, but you can make out the letters, carved into the wood rather than painted: OLD GALLERY 4. Below it, someone has scratched a second line in charcoal, newer but still faded: PLAYED OUT.

Beyond the doors, your light catches the edge of a wide chamber. You can see the remains of old timber supports and what looks like collapsed rubble blocking most of the passage further in. It's been abandoned for a long time.

You move back to the branch and crouch, holding the lantern low to the ground. The stone floor is coated in a fine layer of dust and stone powder. You can see boot prints leading into the right-hand passage. They're not perfectly clear, the dust having shifted somewhat, but you can make out at least two different sets of prints heading down the steep passage, going in. The prints are concentrated near the walls, as if the walkers were keeping close to the stone for support on the steep descent. You don't see any prints coming back out.

The cold draft from the right passage tugs at your beard, carrying that stale, old smell.

What do you do?

I follow the prints down the right passage, keeping close to the wall like the miners did, shield up and lantern held low so I can keep watching the tracks. I'll go slowly on the steep slope and stop at once if the prints change or I see any of those walking lights.

input.text:
Apologies for the confusion! Let me set the scene properly from the start.

The world is one of deep stone and cold iron, where the old gods are honoured in mountain temples and the mineshafts run dark and long beneath the peaks. Greyhollow is a mining town carved into a frost-bitten mountainside, and its people know the mountain's moods better than most. Brakka Ironvein, a hill dwarf fighter, has spent the last six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father there, keeping watch over the faithful and the forge-fires alike.

Three days ago, three miners descended into the North Works, the old galleries sealed off a generation ago. None returned. Last night a fourth man stumbled out of the dark alone, raving about lights that walk, and died before dawn. The town council has decided to brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. But Prior Hessa, the old dwarf who leads the temple, asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back.

It is late afternoon on the tenth of Frost. Brakka stands at the mine mouth, a hooded lantern borrowed from the temple in one hand. The opening is a rough-cut arch in the mountainside, old timber framing blackened with age. A cold draft breathes out from the darkness beyond, carrying the faint smell of wet stone and something else, something stale and old. The tracks of the mine cart rails vanish into the black. Behind Brakka, the grey light of a fading autumn day.

What does Brakka do?

input.text:
You kneel at the mine mouth, lantern set down for a moment, and study the ground. The stone dust and gravel show signs of passage, but the tracks are muddled. You can make out the parallel grooves of the mine cart rails, and there are boot prints, but they overlap and smear where several people have walked back and forth. You can tell that multiple people entered recently, heading in, but the exact number and whether any came back out is hard to say from here.

You light the hooded lantern. Its warm glow pushes back the shadows, the shuttered beam casting a cone of amber light ahead. Shield raised, you step onto the cart rails and begin to walk into the mountain.

The air cools immediately. The smell is stronger now, that stale, old scent like a sealed room left for decades. Your boots crunch on the gravel between the rails. The timber supports pass overhead in a rhythm, some newer and some so old the wood has turned grey and soft. The walls are rough-cut stone, glistening with moisture in the lantern light. The tunnel slopes gently downward, curving slightly to the left.

After about fifty feet, the tunnel opens into a small chamber where two passages branch off. To the left, the tunnel continues, and you can see old timber doors hanging open, marked with a faded sign. To the right, a narrower passage descends more steeply, and from it comes a faint, cold draft carrying that stale smell more strongly.

The lantern light flickers in the draft. What do you do?

input.text:
You step to the left passage and hold the lantern up to the timber doors. The wood is old and warped, hanging crooked on rusted hinges. Above them, a wooden sign is nailed to the frame. The paint has mostly peeled away, but you can make out the letters, carved into the wood rather than painted: OLD GALLERY 4. Below it, someone has scratched a second line in charcoal, newer but still faded: PLAYED OUT.

Beyond the doors, your light catches the edge of a wide chamber. You can see the remains of old timber supports and what looks like collapsed rubble blocking most of the passage further in. It's been abandoned for a long time.

You move back to the branch and crouch, holding the lantern low to the ground. The stone floor is coated in a fine layer of dust and stone powder. You can see boot prints leading into the right-hand passage. They're not perfectly clear, the dust having shifted somewhat, but you can make out at least two different sets of prints heading down the steep passage, going in. The prints are concentrated near the walls, as if the walkers were keeping close to the stone for support on the steep descent. You don't see any prints coming back out.

The cold draft from the right passage tugs at your beard, carrying that stale, old smell.

What do you do?
